query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys (HEAs) that are initially supersaturated solid solutions, low-temperature diffusion during post-solidification aging drives Mg redistribution and precipitation of Mg-rich and Al–X (X = Ti, Zn, Sn, Cu, rare-earth) intermetallics. This chemical partitioning simultaneously (i) increases micro-galvanic heterogeneity at the alloy/electrolyte interface, degrading chloride corrosion resistance relative to the as-quenched baseline, and (ii) lowers the Mg activity of the matrix near the surface, promoting faster establishment of a continuous Al2O3/MgAl2O4-rich scale (instead of porous MgO) during high-temperature oxidation, thereby improving oxidation resistance relative to the as-quenched baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: A Mg-containing lightweight HEA (e.g., Al–Mg–(Ti/Sn/Zn/Cu/Gd) family) with density < 6 g/cm3, prepared by rapid solidification/solutionizing and quenching to a supersaturated, near-single-phase matrix with minimal coarse intermetallics and a Mg-rich, hydroxylated native film.
generation.intervention: Controlled low-temperature aging that allows diffusion-driven partitioning and precipitation without extensive coarsening (e.g., 250–350 C isothermal hold).
generation.conditions: Aging: 300 C for 24 h in inert gas. Corrosion test: 0.6 M NaCl, pH ~6.5, 25 C, aerated. Oxidation test: dry air at 700–800 C for 10 h. All samples mechanically polished to the same finish and cleaned identically.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of nanoscale-to-submicron precipitates and networks (e.g., MgZn2/Mg2Sn-type Mg-rich phases and Al–X intermetallics such as Al3X/Al2X) and associated Mg depletion of the matrix near the surface and grain boundaries; resulting changes in passive film chemistry (from MgO/Mg(OH)2-rich toward Al2O3/MgAl2O4-rich) and in local galvanic couples between intermetallics and matrix.
generation.mechanism: Thermodynamic driving forces from large atomic size/electronegativity and enthalpy differences cause a supersaturated non-equilibrium matrix to decompose upon mild aging. Mg partitions into Mg-rich intermetallics and/or segregates to interfaces, while Al and transition/rare-earth elements form stable Al–X compounds. This raises the electrochemical potential differences among adjacent phases, increasing local dissolution at Mg-rich or anodic particles and at their particle–matrix interfaces in chloride solution (greater pit initiation and propagation). Concurrently, the Mg-depleted matrix near the free surface exhibits reduced Mg activity, favoring selective outward diffusion of Al and formation of denser Al2O3/MgAl2O4 rather than rapid MgO formation; the resulting scale is more adherent and less permeable, lowering the oxidation rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: - Relative to the as-quenched baseline, the aged alloy will show: (a) corrosion: lower pitting potential and higher corrosion current density in chloride solution; more frequent/ deeper pits initiating at intermetallic–matrix interfaces; (b) oxidation: reduced mass gain and a lower parabolic rate constant at 700–800 C; a transition of the external scale from MgO/Mg(OH)2-rich to Al2O3/MgAl2O4-rich with improved continuity/adherence; (c) microstructure: measurable Mg partitioning and precipitate formation (nanoscale-to-submicron) and corresponding matrix Mg depletion near the surface.
generation.baseline: As-quenched, supersaturated alloy with minimal precipitates and a relatively homogeneous matrix that forms a MgO/Mg(OH)2-rich, porous initial film; exhibits higher pitting potential and lower oxidation resistance compared to the aged state described.
generation.boundary: - The hypothesis applies to Mg-containing lightweight HEAs with sufficient Al to form alumina/spinel and with strong binary/ternary affinities that favor intermetallic precipitation under 250–350 C aging, while maintaining density < 6 g/cm3. It may not hold if: (i) cooling is slow enough that a percolating intermetallic network already exists prior to aging; (ii) Al is too low to form protective alumina/spinel; (iii) aging is too mild (<150 C) to induce partitioning or too severe (>450 C) causing coarsening/percolation that changes galvanic area ratios and scale adhesion; (iv) environments differ markedly (e.g., non-chloride electrolytes for corrosion or oxygen partial pressures/humidity that suppress alumina formation).
generation.uncertainty: While the directions (corrosion worsens, oxidation improves after aging) are predicted, the magnitudes depend on specific composition and precipitate topology. The exact identity and volume fraction of intermetallics (e.g., MgZn2 vs Mg2Sn vs Al3X/Al2X) will vary with alloy system, affecting the size of the changes in pitting potential and oxidation kinetics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare one batch of a representative Mg-containing lightweight HEA. Split into two conditions: (A) as-quenched supersaturated baseline; (B) aged at 300 C for 24 h in argon. Characterize both before exposure, then test corrosion and oxidation as specified.
measurements: Pre/post-aging microstructure: TEM/EDS, APT for Mg partitioning; XRD for precipitate phases; DSC for exotherms of decomposition
Surface composition/film: XPS/ToF-SIMS/GDOES depth profiles after oxidation and after short immersion in NaCl
Electrochemistry: open-circuit potential, potentiodynamic polarization to determine pitting potential and corrosion current; EIS for passive film resistance
Localized corrosion mapping: SVET or SKP and cross-sectional SEM of pits
High-temperature oxidation: TGA mass gain vs time at 750 C; post-oxidation scale cross-sections (SEM/EDS), phase ID (XRD/Raman), adhesion (spallation inspection)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if, despite clear evidence of aging-induced Mg partitioning/precipitation, the aged sample does not show the predicted opposite trends: specifically, if the aged alloy exhibits equal or higher pitting resistance than the as-quenched state in chloride solution and simultaneously equal or worse oxidation kinetics (higher mass gain/parabolic rate constant) with no shift toward a continuous Al2O3/MgAl2O4-rich scale.
